docs.text: Open-source embedded C++ Write the driver once. Run it on any MCU. ¶ Chip drivers and firmware building blocks in C++20 that never call a vendor SDK. Give a driver two small functions for your bus and the same code runs on ESP32, STM32, RP2040 or your laptop, where its tests run without hardware. MIT licensed. Start a driver See what's here GitHub Why it's different ¶ You write the port, not the driver A driver needs two functions from you: bring the bus up, and move bytes. A C++20 concept checks them at compile time, so a missing or wrong hook is a compile error, not a crash on the bench. Tests before the board arrives Every driver builds and runs its tests on the host against a simulated chip. Compile-fail tests prove the port contract rejects what it should. Small and predictable Every call returns Result<T> with an error code. No exceptions, no heap, no RTTI, no virtual calls, so it fits small MCUs and safety reviews. Every repository also comes with the same documentation site, lint, static analysis, sign-off check and one required check, from shared workflows pinned with @v1 . What a port looks like ¶ The whole MCU-specific part of an SPI driver, from driver-template . Fill in the two bodies with your SDK's calls: #include "xmpl100.hpp" class MyPort : public xmpl100 :: SpiInterface < MyPort > { public : bool EnsureInitialized () noexcept ; // bring the bus up on the first call; true at once afterwards bool Transfer ( const uint8_t * tx , uint8_t * rx , std :: size_t len ) noexcept ; // one transfer, CS held low }; Then use the driver the same way on every board: xmpl100 :: XMPL100 < MyPort > sensor ( port ); // no I/O yet if ( auto r = sensor . Initialize (); ! r ) { // bus up, reset, chip ID check return static_cast < int > ( r . error ); // Bus, Timeout or DeviceIdMismatch } const auto t = sensor . ReadTemperatureC (); // t.value in degrees Celsius, or t.error From your firmware to the chip Figure description and sources Top to bottom, each arrow is a call. Your firmware calls the kb-core handlers, which call chip drivers (driver- ), which reach the hardware only through an MCU port, yours or a ready one from kb-core; the port drives the chip on your board. Dashed cards are planned. On the right, the tools that every repository uses: driver-template starts a driver, espidf-tools builds and flashes ESP-IDF projects, ci-tools checks, documents and releases them all. docs.text: Contributing ¶ Good first contributions ¶ You can Where Fix a doc, a typo or a broken example Any repository; the docs live in docs/ Ask for a driver, or say which chip you need most Driver request Write a driver for a chip you know Start from driver-template and open a discussion first Write a port for an MCU we don't cover yet Open a discussion ; ports go in kb-core Report a bug The repository's issues, with the bug form Issues labelled good first issue are a good start. How a change gets in ¶ Fork the repository and create a branch. Make the change, with its docs and tests in the same pull request. Sign off every commit: git commit -s . CI fails a pull request with a commit that has no matching Signed-off-by: line. Open the pull request. CI gate runs every check and tells you what is missing; a maintainer reviews. Workflows from a first-time contributor's fork wait for a maintainer's approval before they run. Security ¶ Report a vulnerability privately through the repository's Security tab ("Report a vulnerability"), never in a public issue. The security policy says what happens next. Community ¶ Be kind and specific: the code of conduct applies everywhere. Full details are in the contributing guide .

docs.text: How we build ¶ A driver never touches the SDK ¶ A driver is the chip's datasheet turned into C++: registers, timing, modes and errors. Everything that depends on your MCU sits behind a small port class that you write, and the driver only calls its hooks. The driver owns Your port owns Register framing, reset and chip-ID checks, conversions, CRCs Bringing the bus up, moving bytes, optional GPIO, delay and log hooks Units, ranges and Config presets with datasheet defaults Pins, clocks, DMA, locking, which SPI or I2C peripheral The port derives from the driver's interface with CRTP ( class MyPort : public chip::SpiInterface<MyPort> ) and a C++20 concept checks every required hook at compile time. There are no virtual calls, so the compiler can inline the port into the driver. Predictable on small MCUs ¶ No exceptions, no heap, no RTTI. Every call returns Result<T> : a value, or an Error that says what went wrong ( Bus , Timeout , DeviceIdMismatch , chip-specific faults). Nothing happens in a constructor. Initialize() does the first I/O, so you decide when the bus is touched. Bounded waits. A driver never blocks forever on a busy flag. Brand-free ¶ A driver is named after its chip, not after a product: repository driver-<chip> , namespace <chip>:: . A product's pin map or modes never go into a shared repository. Kind of "specific" Example Where it lives Chip-specific the registers of one sensor that chip's driver MCU-specific an ESP-IDF SPI port interfaces/mcu/<family>/ in kb-core, built only for that family Product-specific one product's pin map or modes the product's own repository, through extension points Tested without hardware ¶ Every driver builds and runs its tests on the host with CMake and ctest : a simulated chip answers like the real one, error paths are forced, and compile-fail tests check that a broken port does not compile. Hardware tests are labelled needs-hardware and hardware-verified on pull requests. The same checks in every repository ¶ Check What it catches Strict docs build, link check, figure and generated-table drift Broken links, stale diagrams, docs that disagree with the code Host build and tests, clang-tidy, cppcheck Bugs, undefined behaviour, the port contract clang-format, markdownlint, yamllint Style drift DCO sign-off, required files, MIT licence Provenance and licensing CI gate One required check that passes only when everything else did Supply-chain hygiene ¶ Every third-party GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA on a real release tag and reviewed before it is allowed in the organisation; tools without a trusted action are downloaded from their own release and checked against a pinned SHA-256. Dependabot keeps the pins current. Secret scanning with push protection, Dependabot alerts and CodeQL are on for every repository. Licence and sign-off ¶ Everything is MIT licensed, Copyright (c) 2026 The Kokeb Labs Authors . There is no CLA: you sign off each commit ( git commit -s ) to certify the Developer Certificate of Origin .

docs.text: Projects ¶ Every repository is public, MIT licensed and checked by the same CI: a strict docs build, lint, the DCO sign-off and one required check, CI gate . driver-template Ready ¶ Start a new chip driver or library in one command. Create a repository from the template, run python3 tools/setup.py , answer a few questions (chip name, bus, description), and you get: A C++20 driver skeleton for an SPI, I2C or UART chip, or a header-only library, with the port contract checked by a concept at compile time. Host tests against a simulated chip, compile-fail tests for the port contract, and an optimised-build check. A host example that runs on your PC, and an ESP32 example built by espidf-tools . A documentation site with the layer figure drawn from your headers, and the full CI. Repository Using the template espidf-tools v1 ¶ Build, flash and monitor every app of a multi-app ESP-IDF project. List the apps, ESP-IDF versions, build types and target once in app_config.yml ; the same scripts run on your machine and in CI. build_app.sh and flash_app.sh for any app, build type and ESP-IDF version, each built into its own folder. manage_idf.sh installs and switches ESP-IDF versions; serial-port detection, logs and tab completion included. generate_matrix.py turns app_config.yml into a CI matrix, so CI builds exactly what you build locally. Documentation Repository ci-tools v1 ¶ The CI and documentation platform every repository uses. Short caller workflows pin @v1 and get fixes without breaking changes. C++ build and host tests, clang-format, clang-tidy and cppcheck over one compile database. ESP-IDF firmware builds across versions and build types with a size report, and releases that ship the exact firmware CI built. The documentation theme and figure kit used on this site: light and dark from one layout, contrast-checked, and redrawn from the code so a figure can't go stale. Every third-party action pinned to a commit SHA and reviewed before it is allowed. Documentation Repository .github ¶ The organisation's profile, community files (contributing, code of conduct, security policy), the brand, and the settings of every repository kept as code. Repository Coming next Next ¶ Chip drivers , one repository per chip, named driver-<chip> , moving in from HardFOC. kb-core : MCU interfaces with ESP32, STM32 and host ports, a small RTOS layer, utilities, and the handlers that join drivers to the interfaces. See the roadmap for the order, or request a driver . Boards ¶ HardFOC is a family of motor-control boards built on these drivers and tools. It keeps its own organisation; Kokeb Labs holds the parts that work on any board.

Chip drivers Next Drivers move in from HardFOC one chip at a time, renamed driver-<chip> , each with host tests, an ESP32 example and a docs site. kb-core One repository with kb::utils , kb::rtos , kb::interfaces and kb::handlers . HardFOC on Kokeb The HardFOC motor-control boards build on these drivers and kb-core. Tools for users A command-line tool, a board configurator and a documentation hub.
